doc.title: Ray Ricker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 27, 2022

title: Phil Woods's advice to young players and Ricker's reaction
summary: Ricker responds to Woods's advice that jazz is only for those with no choice, and advises a grandchild to know technology and the world stage.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: I have a — speaking of previous interviews, I want to read something from two individuals and just get your reaction to it. This is from Phil Woods, and I was able to speak with him, probably — I’ve lost track — fifteen years or so. And I asked him about advice for young jazz men. And he said, “I think jazz is only for those that have no choice. I think if you’re a young man and you’re entertaining thoughts of becoming a brain surgeon or a jazz tenor man, I’d go with the brain surgery. If you’ve got two burning desires don’t pick jazz. Don’t rush into a jazz school or any university. I recommend taking a year off, hitchhike around the world, take your horn and see if you can play for your supper.

Well that’s very good advice, really. I think to be — if you just look at it you know you can start thinking pretty gloomy things about even being a music major let alone being a jazz musician. But the thing is that if you take what you do to the highest possible level and if you are successful being a really fine player, people recognize that and they will you know pay for you to play. But it’s really tough, I mean some of the jazz guys going to New York nowadays, it’s not $15 they’re playing for but it’s not much more. You know? Maybe $50 on some of the things you know just doing it to meet people and get started. I’m talking about guys right out of school. So I think what Phil was saying there was if you want to be a musician it has to call you and you can’t think of doing anything else. It really has to be, this is it I’m doing it I’m going for it. You know.
If you had a grandchild who wanted to do it, what would you say to them?

I’d say to them — first of all to — I probably wouldn’t even have to push this at all but know technology. Know what’s going on and how the stage is now so much more than the town that you’re in or the state that you’re in or the country you’re in. It’s all over the world. And you know musicians find good work in Europe and in Asia. You know China is a good example. Jeez I had one guy that came — he went to Oberlin for his undergrad, and then he went to China. And he was in Shanghai for I think two or three years. Some of his other buddies were there. And they worked. They worked just playing American stuff you know, for Chinese businesses. And then he came back and he had all that

experience playing and a very fine player and he got a master’s degree here and he’s now down in the D.C. area. But, yeah, he was thinking more of the world than just here, just what am I going to do? How can I get another job in Rochester? You know. Well you know maybe you’ve got to get the technology thing happening and become a very fine player, that’s for sure.
